name: Producerism
summary: Producerism holds that those who make tangible wealth, such as farmers, artisans and wage workers, are the virtuous core of society and are exploited by idle or parasitic groups, above all bankers, monopolists, land speculators and aristocrats. It demands that government be taken back from corrupt elites and used to curb concentrated wealth through public money, public ownership of key networks and land for actual settlers. Critics note that the producer ideal was often racialized and gendered and that later strands aim the 'parasite' label at the poor below as well as elites above.
scope: The 19th-century American strand at its peak: the Knights of Labor preamble (1878) and the People's Party Omaha Platform (1892), with roots in the Jacksonian producing classes and the British Radical tradition. Modern right-populist uses (Perot, Buchanan, Trump, Le Pen) are noted but not modelled, and most statements outside economics, land, money, democracy and immigration are low-confidence inferences.

keyFigures.name: Eugene V. Debs
keyFigures.role: Led the 1894 Pullman Strike, which some commentators see as the high-water mark of American producerism.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Gilded Age producerists never addressed health care; their demand for state action is aimed at railroads, money and land, so the answer is split.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: No minimum wage existed, but the Knights wanted full weekly wages and a fair share for workers, which suggests support for a floor.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Omaha Platform treats unregulated markets as rigged by monopolies, banks and railroads, and calls for state ownership of key networks.

public-ownership.rationale: Omaha demands government ownership and operation of railroads, telegraph and telephone, though energy and other utilities go unmentioned.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Omaha demands a graduated income tax aimed at idle accumulated wealth, though the size of the rise is not specified.

unions-good.rationale: The Knights of Labor were a labor organization built to unite all productive workers, and Omaha affirms the right to organize and condemns Pinkerton force.

property-fundamental.rationale: Producerists defend the earnings and holdings of the producer, but Omaha also reclaims railroad and foreign-held land, so property is not treated as untouchable.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Omaha says the nation is near ruin from corporate power and demands that railroads be owned by the public or regulated into serving it.

cut-welfare.rationale: Modern producerism resents supporting non-producers, but the Gilded Age strand focused on idle wealth above rather than the poor below, so adherents split.

worker-ownership.rationale: The Knights called for producer and distributive co-operatives, which points to workers owning their enterprises, though not as a universal program.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Nothing in the sources bears on surveillance; the producerist focus is economic, and populists were wary of both elites and state power.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Drug policy lies outside producerist doctrine and the movement drew both temperance and libertarian supporters.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Inferred from the plain-people populist distrust of established institutions; speech limits were not discussed and 19th-century producerists favored open agitation.

strong-leader.rationale: Omaha limits presidents to one term and extends direct election, signalling suspicion of concentrated executive power.

state-harmful.rationale: Omaha wants the people's power of government expanded to end oppression and poverty, the opposite of an anti-state view.

limit-guns.rationale: Inferred from the Jacksonian and agrarian republican tradition that valued armed independent citizens; gun control was not a platform issue.

empower-police-military.rationale: The Knights and Populists feared private armies and strike-breaking forces, so more coercive state power was not a priority.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Producerism's moral register about virtuous work and the republican family suggests disapproval, but sources are silent on it.

decide-locally.rationale: Populism grew from local farmer organizations and directly elected officials, but Omaha also demands national action on money and railroads.

rehabilitation.rationale: The Knights opposed convict contract labor, but there is no evidence on punishment philosophy.

traditional-family.rationale: Scholarship notes the producer ideal rested on gendered, household notions of independence; the platforms did not address the family directly.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Inferred from 19th-century conventional morals and the producer image of a male household head; not discussed in sources.

abortion-legal.rationale: Inferred from conventional moral views of the era; the sources say nothing on abortion.

more-religion-public.rationale: Populism had evangelical rhetoric but also anti-Catholic and secular strands; no unified stance.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The producer ideal centered the white male citizen, and many Populists backed exclusion, though some urged biracial cooperation; active remedies were not on the agenda.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Producerism rested on gendered notions of the producer, so a constructionist view was foreign to it.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Populists defended the native-born plain people and anti-Catholic currents were present, but culture was secondary to economics.

gradual-change.rationale: Omaha opens by declaring the nation on the verge of ruin and demands sweeping changes to money, land and transport.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Omaha calls for further restriction of immigration and of contract labor, citing wage undercutting.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Omaha attacks foreign influence over finance; international bodies did not exist but producerists favored home control of money.

free-trade.rationale: Omaha dismisses the major parties' tariff fight as a sham, so adherents did not hold free trade as a creed nor endorse it.

nation-first.rationale: Producerists focus on the nation's own working people and oppose foreign ownership of land, but they did not frame it as against global cooperation.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Inferred from the agrarian focus on domestic reform; no doctrine on foreign intervention.

open-borders.rationale: Omaha opposes open ports for impoverished and criminal foreigners who undercut wages.

limit-growth.rationale: Producerism celebrates the production of wealth; environmental limits were not an issue of the era.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic; producerists neither deny nor prioritize it, and modern strands vary.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Omaha praises productive industry but also sees concentrated corporate power as technology's problem.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic for the Gilded Age strand; modern producerist politicians tend to back domestic energy production, but there is no doctrine.

revolution-justified.rationale: Populists sought change through elections and a new party, though Omaha's language is angry; revolution was not advocated.

experts-over-public.rationale: Omaha insists the plain people retake control of government, and direct election and ballot reforms express trust in ordinary voters over elites.

central-planning.rationale: Omaha favors state ownership of a few networks and government credit, but not a planned economy replacing markets for farmers and artisans.

socialized-markets.rationale: The Knights favored co-operatives, but the proprietary producerist strand valued private small owners, so views were split.

land-value-tax.rationale: The Georgist single tax was part of British producerism, but the American Omaha program used graduated income tax instead, so adherents are split.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Producerism condemns wealth gained without labor, including aristocratic inheritance, but sources give no tax program.

basic-income.rationale: Income for non-producers cuts against the producerist idea that rewards flow from work.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Omaha calls the tariff a sham battle and says protective tariffs fail to protect workers.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Omaha proposes government credit and sub-treasury loans to farmers, but not strategic industrial planning.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Producerism holds that wealth belongs to those who make it; both platforms reserve land for actual settlers rather than speculators and corporations.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The Knights demanded full weekly wages in lawful money and equal pay, treating wage labor as legitimate if fairly paid.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Omaha wants national currency issued by government, so no market money, though it also rejects private banking control.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The Knights favored arbitration of disputes, but state-recognized wage and price bodies were not proposed.

one-party-rule.rationale: Populists formed a competing party for fair elections and a secret ballot; one-party rule contradicts that.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Producerism's roots are in opposition to aristocratic idleness and the Radical tradition against the few.

democracy-best.rationale: Omaha aims to restore government to the plain people through direct election and reforms, though voters choosing badly is not discussed.

direct-votes.rationale: The party added initiative and referendum to its program at its 1896 convention.

workers-councils.rationale: Producerists pursued electoral politics and direct election reforms, not councils replacing parliaments.

right-to-secede.rationale: Populists sought to take over the national government; nothing indicates support for secession.

natural-rulers.rationale: Producerism rejects aristocracy and rule by birth in favor of those who work.

political-violence-never.rationale: Knights preferred arbitration over strikes and Populists used elections, but Omaha fears and condemns private armed force, not all violence.

war-builds-character.rationale: Inferred from the producerist glorification of productive labor, not battle; the platforms are silent on war.

separate-church-state.rationale: Populists included evangelicals and anti-Catholic activists as well as freethinkers; no common stance.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Religious rhetoric appeared but the platform is secular economic reform.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Omaha condemns private armed forces like the Pinkertons and wants public control of key services.

military-superiority.rationale: The platforms never discuss military power, and Populists mixed isolationists with 1898 expansionists.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Some white Populists backed exclusion, while others urged biracial farmer cooperation, so views were split.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Producerism sees conflict between producers and parasites, which is not the Marxist class view, and it stresses cooperation among producing classes.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The Knights wanted fair shares for labor, but reward by work implies unequal outcomes by contribution.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Populist land policy reserved land for settlers; indigenous claims were not part of the program.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Inferred from the movement's concern with domestic farmers and workers; it does not discuss colonial debts.

civilizational-union.rationale: Inferred from the national scope of the Omaha program; supranational civilizational unions are absent.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The Knights set industrial and moral worth rather than wealth as the measure of greatness, rejecting acquisitiveness as a virtue.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Republican virtue discourse stresses civic duty, but there is no stated rule for ranking duties and rights.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Anachronistic; land was treated as the people's inheritance but for human settlers.

limit-population.rationale: Inferred from the producerist emphasis on settlement of land by actual settlers, which welcomes more producers.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Omaha celebrates productive industry and wants it freed of monopoly rather than abandoned.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Producerists celebrate productive industry but resent concentrated capital using it against workers, so views split.

human-enhancement.rationale: Anachronistic; producerism values honest labor and offers no guidance on bodily technology, so adherents split between enthusiasm for progress and wariness.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement's demand for popular control over government points against it.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Anachronistic; neither platform touches communications privacy, and producerist distrust of both elites and state power points both ways.

restore-past-order.rationale: Producerists look back to republican artisan and yeoman independence but also demand new reforms, so they are split.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Omaha is programmatic, but populists were pragmatic about fusion on free silver, so evidence is mixed.

direct-action.rationale: Populists organized as a political party contesting elections and demanding ballot reform.

means-match-ends.rationale: The Omaha program seeks electoral and legislative change without a stated theory that methods must prefigure the goal, so this is a genuine blank.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Producerism celebrates farming, industry and productive work, not primitivism.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The Knights sought to unite every department of productive industry, accepting specialized trades.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Producerists reward work: the Knights wanted workers to get the full fruit of their labor.

production-for-use.rationale: Co-operatives were favored, but profit by honest producers was not condemned, so views split.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Industrial producerism condemned unearned gain by speculators, while proprietary producerism accepted profit from one's own enterprise.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Producerists organized across wage workers, farmers and small owners and sought electoral reform, not dictatorship over classes.

collective-farming.rationale: The program reserved land for individual settlers and small farmers.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Producerists attack bankers and monopolists, not capitalism as a system, and war is not in their platforms.

taxation-theft.rationale: Omaha demands a graduated income tax and expansion of government's role.

harm-principle.rationale: Producerists were mostly moral reformers who accepted temperance and morals legislation alongside anti-monopoly measures, so this liberal rule does not map onto them.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Producerism speaks of producing classes as groups with shared interests while also stressing individual desert, so it does not take either side.

conscription.rationale: Inferred from the Populist wariness of coercive state and private armed force; conscription is not discussed.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Omaha puts popular political control above all, with direct election and ballot reform as the check on government.

state-as-business.rationale: Populists wanted government run for the people, not as a business, and favored public ownership of networks.

positive-liberty.rationale: The Knights demanded leisure, fair wages and settlement land as conditions of real independence.

media-academia-power.rationale: Modern producerists often attack media and academics, but the Gilded Age strand did not.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Racial thinking varied among Populists; sources give no stated doctrine on genetic ability.

organic-representation.rationale: Omaha demands direct election and ballot reform, not representation through bodies.

total-state.rationale: Omaha's state role is limited to money, transport and land; it does not direct culture.

national-rebirth.rationale: Omaha speaks of national ruin and rescue, but no rebirth myth.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Inferred from the platforms' exclusive concern with domestic money, land and railroads; some Populists backed 1890s expansion but the program does not.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Rejects aristocratic patronage in favor of producing classes.

bound-labor.rationale: Knights demanded full wages and abolition of contract labor; bound labor is opposite.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Anachronistic; Enlightenment-republican producerists would not share it.

universal-morality.rationale: The Knights ground their platform on moral worth rather than wealth, implying shared moral truths, but not stated as epistemology.

single-common-good.rationale: The Knights speak of the greatest good for the greatest number and of a single producing interest against its enemies.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Anachronistic for the 1890s; the movement had no Zionist position, and its record on Jews is itself disputed by historians.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Not a producerist issue; the sources contain no view on diaspora rights, and the immigration planks are restrictive but not about descent.

revive-national-language.rationale: No language politics appear in the Omaha or Knights platforms, and nothing in producerist principle bears on it.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Co-operative production implies workers' say in the firm, but not stated as a program for large companies.

school-vouchers.rationale: Anachronistic; public provision favored for general interest.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Omaha demands expansion of the money supply to relieve falling prices, an expansionary stance.

economic-freedom.rationale: Producerists want freedom from monopoly rather than laissez-faire, so the statement is hard to map.

rule-by-example.rationale: Omaha demands structural reform, such as direct election and ballot secrecy, to bind rulers, which implies distrust of reliance on rulers' virtue.

national-self-determination.rationale: The program sought home rule over money and land; it is not an issue they addressed with respect to other peoples.

force-without-un.rationale: Anachronistic since no UN existed, and the platforms never address using force abroad.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Populist ranks mixed evangelical Protestants with freethinkers, so adherents did not agree on reason versus faith.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Omaha opposes immigrants undercutting native workers, so reserving benefits is consistent though benefits were not discussed.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Producerism makes work the basis of desert, so able-bodied recipients would be expected to work.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Knights and Populists treated farmers, workers and honest employers as one producing class against monopolists and speculators; they preferred arbitration to strikes.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Producerism is conservative about inherited republican values, not a modernist avant-garde.

dominated-front.rationale: Inferred from the producerist focus on the nation's own farmers and workers; anti-Western-front politics would be foreign to a US producerist.

workers-nation.rationale: Producerism defines producers within the nation and opposes immigrant labor competition, though the Knights had some internationalist links.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Knights demanded equal pay for equal work but producerism had gendered ideals; sources split.

ban-interest.rationale: Populists attacked usurious lenders and demanded low-interest credit, not abolition of interest.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Southern Populists were divided between biracial cooperation and support for white supremacy.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Omaha says government was captured by corporate interests but should be retaken, a partial agreement.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Anachronistic; modern right producerists favor it, but there is no doctrine.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Omaha opposes impoverished and contract immigrants but does not set cultural conditions.

elite-replacement.rationale: Omaha blames employers for contract immigrant labor, but the replacement theory is a later development.

proportional-representation.rationale: Omaha focuses on direct election and ballot secrecy; PR was not discussed.

national-mission.rationale: Some Populists shared the era's expansionist rhetoric while others opposed empire, so adherents are split; the platforms are silent.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Producerist ideal was the male household head; structural patriarchy not recognized.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Omaha states the nation is on the verge of moral and political ruin from corruption, with bribed legislatures and parties.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenic policy emerged after the platforms and is absent from them; producerist trust in ordinary families suggests mild opposition.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The Knights and Omaha condemned the Pinkerton system, but accountability for past state killings is a later issue the sources never raise.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Omaha demands state ownership and expansion of government power.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Southern Populists split between biracial farmer cooperation and white supremacy, and the platforms contain no marriage policy.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Scholarship stresses the producer ideal was racialized and gendered, but the platforms' rhetoric of the plain people claimed universal political equality.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist debate with no counterpart in producerism, which is not a socialist doctrine.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Populists championed the settler farmer; the colonial framing is not theirs.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: A religious-law question from South Asia that producerist sources never address.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Anti-Catholicism was present in some Populist circles but no restriction on conversion.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Producerists were commercial farmers and stockmen, so a ban on slaughtering cattle would cut against their own trade.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Populists included both anti-Catholic activists and secular reformers, who would answer differently; the platforms say nothing.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A socialist-state doctrine; producerists hold the state should serve the people and do not expect it to be strengthened for its own survival.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Omaha restores the people's control of government as the people's own power, with ballot reform to secure consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Omaha attacks tariff politics as a sham but sets no goal for the trade balance, so the sources give nothing to infer from.

population-transfer.rationale: Omaha restricts future immigration and alien land ownership but proposes no expulsion of existing residents.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Producerists condemned private armed force against workers but accepted state coercion such as taxation and public ownership, so the absolute rule does not fit.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The Knights emphasize cooperation and moral worth over struggle.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Populists were an insurgent third party and would oppose banning parties.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The Omaha line that corporations will own the people unless the people own them expresses fear of domination by concentrated power.

separated-powers.rationale: Omaha proposes direct election of senators but does not address separation.

vanguard-party.rationale: Producerists were mass-membership, democratic and rejected rule by an elect.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Producerism prioritizes those who produce, including poor farmers and laborers, but sets itself against non-producing poor as well, so adherents are split.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Council housing did not exist; the producerist small-property ideal supports home ownership while public provision cuts the other way.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The Knights preferred arbitration over strikes but did not seek legal restrictions; Omaha supports workers' organizing.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Omaha attributes poverty to monopoly, finance and corruption, not population.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Modern producerism often says so; the Gilded Age sources are split.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Populists favored elections and direct election of senators, not sortition.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Populists complained of bribed and intimidated electorates and demanded secure ballots, so they distrusted suspending legal protections.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Omaha and the Alliance wanted government control of railroad rates and credit but did not propose fixing food prices, which farmers sell.

party-controls-media.rationale: Omaha demands fair and free ballots and popular control, not party control of media.

party-commands-army.rationale: Omaha wants a party built on popular election and condemns private armed bodies like the Pinkertons; party command of the army contradicts civilian democratic control.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Omaha demands stricter immigration controls, which suggests tough naturalization.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Populist plain-people rhetoric suggests sympathy for modest officials, but no pay plank exists.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Populists attacked party machines and wanted direct voter control, so binding discipline is doubtful, but the sources do not discuss it.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Anachronistic; opposition to foreign control of money suggests resistance.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Omaha limits presidents to one term, signalling wariness of executive power.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Populist members were mostly Protestants of differing church orders, so there is no collective view of church government.

clerical-rule.rationale: Omaha is a secular reform program based on popular sovereignty.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: This is a Leninist stance; producerists define themselves as the nation's productive citizens, so working for their own government's defeat is unlikely.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Producerism's moral register about virtuous labor might support censorship, but the movement also valued free agitation, and the sources show nothing.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Omaha explicitly demands that the president and vice president be limited to a single term.

recall-officials.rationale: The party added initiative and referendum, and recall fits their direct democracy but is not mentioned in the source.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Inferred from the platform's exclusive focus on domestic reform; entanglements abroad are not part of it.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Producerism defends small owners but nothing supports banning rentals.

people-in-arms.rationale: Republican tradition valorizes citizens' militias but not in platforms.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Populism was a farmer movement valuing the agrarian producer, though not explicit.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: No divided-nation issue appears in the sources.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Producerist rhetoric elevates plain working people over idle elites.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Racial and cultural hierarchy was widespread among white Populists while biracial cooperation existed too, and the platforms are silent.

death-penalty.rationale: Capital punishment was not a Populist platform issue and no source records a collective stance.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the conventional morals and gendered household ideal associated with the producer image.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Evangelical Populists might say yes, but the 1890s program ignores schooling, so adherents are split.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Producerist moral rhetoric might favor restriction, but the platforms never touch obscenity and the movement was mainly economic.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Omaha restricts immigration but does not address birthright citizenship.

minority-language-support.rationale: Inferred from the native-born, wage-protecting immigration planks, which suggest little support for public programs for other languages.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The platforms are silent and producerism has no theory of religious liberty.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Inferred from the producer ideal's emphasis on steady virtuous work and conventional republican character, not from a stated rule.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Omaha's sympathy for debtors versus creditors suggests support, but international debt not addressed.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Omaha ties political republic to economic reform of money, land and railroads.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Omaha amends the constitution through ordinary reforms such as direct election of senators, and says nothing of a constituent assembly.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Omaha puts a free and fair ballot at the head of its demands, so trading away political freedoms for growth contradicts its program.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Domestic focus; producerists oppose transfers to non-producers.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Anachronistic; nothing in producerism bears on nuclear weapons.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Omaha wants direct election of senators and one-term president, which suggests popular selection.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Omaha wants money issued by the federal government and not by banking corporations.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: No territorial dispute features in the sources.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Omaha calls land the people's inheritance and reclaims excess railroad holdings for settlers.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A debate internal to Marxism that producerists did not take part in.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Anachronistic; producerism celebrates productive output and has no environmental risk doctrine.

collective-defense.rationale: Anachronistic; the platforms contain no foreign alliances, and later populist producerists are wary of entanglements.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: No annexation issue appears in the sources.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Populists were largely Protestant; they did not push to restrain church property or clergy, and the sources record no stance.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The US presidency is partisan, and Populists wanted that office limited rather than turned ceremonial, so the question does not map.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The sources do not address secession, and producerists would likely split along regional lines.

region-keeps-system.rationale: No regional autonomy arrangements appear in the sources.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Producerism arose as opposition to the aristocracy and to rule by birth, so a sacred hereditary ruler is incompatible with it.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Omaha demands a graduated income tax, which is incompatible with equal rates.

character-from-environment.rationale: The Knights stress the moral worth of labor, but nothing in the sources addresses nature versus upbringing.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Omaha aims to return government to the plain people and subject officials to their control, rejecting unbound rulers.

space-expansion.rationale: Anachronistic; nothing in producerism bears on space.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Omaha leans toward direct popular rule over mixed rule by the few.

leader-cult.rationale: Omaha limits the president to one term and stresses popular power, which is opposed to personal veneration of leaders.

equal-parenting.rationale: Anachronistic; the gendered household ideal does not imply a view on custody presumptions.

land-redistribution.rationale: Omaha wants land held by railroads and corporations in excess of need reclaimed and given to actual settlers.

refugee-return.rationale: No refugee or return question appears in the sources.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Producerists had no irredentist program in the sources.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Omaha is a secular economic and political reform program, and punishing leaving a religion would sit outside it and against its constitutional tradition.

women-must-cover.rationale: The program is secular and civic, and producerist agitation had women active in the party and unions.

common-currency.rationale: Omaha wants national money issued by the federal government; supranational unions are foreign to it.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: No pan-ethnic unity appears in the sources.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: A multiethnic-empire doctrine with no counterpart in the sources.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Not a producerist matter, and the sources do not discuss minority emigration.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Producerists emphasize moral struggle between producers and parasites rather than historical materialism.

ban-cartels.rationale: Omaha attacks monopolies, calls for government control of railroads, and supports breaking up concentrated economic power.

no-bailouts.rationale: Producerism denounces bankers living off others' labor, so public rescues of failing banks would be opposed, though not discussed in the 1890s.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Omaha's emphasis on popular power over elites suggests impatience with judicial constraints, but not stated.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Inferred from the gendered household ideal underlying the producer image; the Knights sought equal pay but not mandated representation.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Omaha attacks protective tariffs as a sham but also restricts foreign land ownership, so an autarkic bloc is neither supported nor excluded.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Anachronistic; the Knights wanted labor standards at home, but trade agreements did not exist.

moral-incentives.rationale: The Knights demand fair pay for work; incentives by wage are accepted.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The cited sources never discuss revolutionary strategy. Populists organised a mass party to win elections, and the Omaha Platform (s2) condemns private armed forces used against workers, so disagreement is inferred.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The producerist tradition arose in opposition to the aristocracy living on others' work.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Some Populists backed 1898 imperial expansion while others opposed it, and the platforms are silent.

patriotic-education.rationale: Populist rhetoric framed the party as restoring the republic, so patriotic civic instruction fits, though no plank states it.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Anachronistic; racial preferences did not exist, and white Populists split on race.

public-money-creation.rationale: Omaha demands that currency be issued only by the federal government without banking corporations as intermediaries, and the Knights platform says the same.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Omaha predicts ruin if its reforms fail, but producerists do not hold a theory of collapse or adaptation of capitalism as such.

former-empire-influence.rationale: No predecessor-empire issue appears in the sources.

delink-world-market.rationale: Not a producerist question; Omaha concerns the home economy only.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Leninist concept absent from producerism.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The Knights organized across trades and sexes with equal pay for equal work, which cuts against unlimited private exclusion, though race is a different question.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Populists wanted more direct democracy, and nothing in the sources addresses amendment barriers.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: No colonial treaty issue appears in the sources.

elective-rulers.rationale: Omaha demands direct election of senators and secret ballots, and producerism opposes rule by birth.

minority-veto.rationale: Omaha pursues majoritarian reforms such as direct election and later initiative and referendum, which leaves no place for a minority veto.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Populist rhetoric of reclaiming the republic from corrupt rulers suggests this, but not explicit.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Anachronistic for the American context; Populists sought to democratize a presidential system.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal welfare is not in the sources; agrarian producers raised animals for use.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Inferred from agrarian producerism, which raises animals for food while not seeking cruelty; no source states it.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Producerism rejects aristocratic patronage; fair payment replaces charity.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Producerism is a mass political movement demanding that the plain people take back government.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: A Frankfurt School argument absent from producerism.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Omaha blames corruption and intimidation rather than cultural hegemony, so there is no stated view.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Omaha's grievances are domestic, between producers and bankers, though foreign ownership of land is criticized.

native-born-offices.rationale: Omaha restricts immigration and alien landholding but does not mention offices.

party-own-road.rationale: A communist-movement question with no counterpart in producerism.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Producerist self-reliance applies to individual producers and sources do not extend it to poor countries.

return-lost-territory.rationale: No lost-territory issue appears in the sources.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Populist land policy served settler farmers, so leadership by descendants of pre-colonial peoples would not be supported.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anachronistic for the 1890s; modern producerist politics diverge.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Anachronistic for the 1890s and no basis in the sources.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Southern and Northern Populists differed in memory of the war and the platform is silent.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Anachronistic for the Gilded Age strand, with no producerist doctrine on memorials.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Anachronistic; producerist focus is on workers rather than on sex-based disadvantage.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Anachronistic and absent from the sources.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: No claim about civilizational differences appears in the sources.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Omaha opposes private armed force and expects civilian democratic control, so a political guardian army is unlikely.

paid-care-work.rationale: Inferred from the gendered household ideal; the producer is a wage earner or farmer, and paid housework is not in the platforms.

filial-duty.rationale: Inferred from the family-centered republican virtue ideal; no source states it.

office-by-exam.rationale: The Knights oppose patronage; Omaha proposes civil service rules for railway workers.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Omaha demands that land held by aliens and foreign syndicates be reclaimed, so blocking foreign purchase of strategic firms extends the same logic, though industrial firms are not named.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Anachronistic and not discussed; temperance-minded Populists and secular reformers might differ.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Initiative and referendum point to binding the representatives.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Anachronistic; Omaha wants postal savings and federal credit, which favors public over private financial intermediaries.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Omaha reserves land for actual settlers, which hints at use-based tenure, but it also protects private farms, so adherents are split.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Not discussed; Omaha limits government revenue to necessary expenses but says nothing on budget approval.

single-official-language.rationale: Language policy does not appear in the platforms.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Omaha explicitly demands that alien ownership of land be prohibited and that land held by aliens be reclaimed.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from producerist emphasis on individual desert rather than group outcomes.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The Knights make moral worth rather than wealth the measure of greatness.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Foreign policy is absent from the platforms.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: A Cold War question outside producerism.

corporate-influence.rationale: Omaha laments corruption by corporations of legislatures and the platform's preamble attacks concentrated economic power.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Omaha restricts foreign land ownership but says nothing about funding of NGOs, so only a weak analogy exists.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Anachronistic; sources show no population policy.

residents-only-property.rationale: Omaha bars alien land ownership and favors land for settlers.

job-guarantee.rationale: The Knights wanted fair work and wages, but a state job guarantee is not in the sources, so adherents are split.

democratic-peace.rationale: A political-science claim absent from the sources.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Producerists sought change through law and elections, so denying a general duty to obey conflicts with this.

non-intervention.rationale: Foreign policy is absent from the platforms.

industrial-unions.rationale: The Knights sought to unite every department of productive industry into one organization.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Some Populists embraced Rothschild conspiracy tales, but historians debate how widespread this was.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Producerism rests on the household of the male producer, so ending legal marriage conflicts with it.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Omaha demands fair, open elections, but says nothing about access to records.

local-production.rationale: Omaha criticizes distant railroads and bankers, but does not propose limiting trade to local markets.

informal-organisation.rationale: The Knights and the People's Party built permanent national organizations with constitutions and conventions, the opposite of loose informal groups.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Anachronistic; no international law institutions are discussed.

religious-nation.rationale: Some Populists framed themselves in evangelical terms, but the platform defines the people by work rather than religion.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Tribute to a leading power contradicts the Omaha demand that the people govern their own affairs.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Farmers resented eastern finance but no plank concerns where regional revenue is spent.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The Knights defend the producer's earnings and tools; this statement matches the proprietary producerist respect for small property.

defeat-communism.rationale: Anachronistic; producerists predate the Soviet Union, and the sources have no such view.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Omaha prefers public ownership of rail and telegraph, but a mixed-provider system is not discussed.

religion-illusion.rationale: Inferred from the Protestant moral rhetoric in much of Populist culture; not stated in the platforms.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Producerists praise productive industry but denounce finance and monopoly, so a verdict on capitalism as such is split.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Knights asked for equal pay for equal work, but not for broader economic transformation of gender relations.

socialized-care.rationale: Inferred from the family-based household ideal of the producer; public provision of housework is absent from the platforms.

purge-loanwords.rationale: No language purism in the sources.

treaties-binding.rationale: Treaty questions regarding indigenous nations are not covered in the sources.

cooperative-communities.rationale: The Knights favored co-operatives but not communal property.

majority-settlement.rationale: No platform or source addresses settling majority-group members in minority regions; Omaha's settler land policy is about farmers, not ethnic groups.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Producerism claims a middle way between finance capital and socialism, favoring small owners and co-operatives, though adherents do not use this phrase.

historical-land-claim.rationale: No historical claim to land appears in the sources.

holocaust-denial.rationale: No producerist source asserts it, and its association with the Gilded Age strand is absent; adherents who cast Jews as financiers still did not deny a later event.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: No platform addresses it, and adherents' view cannot be inferred beyond the era's general conventions.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Omaha demands a fair ballot and organizes an opposition party, so suppression of opposition is opposed.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Some evangelical Populists might favor it, but the platforms never mention it.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Populists split on 1898 empire, and the platforms say nothing about colonies.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Not applicable to a US economic movement.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Omaha locates authority in the people and ballot, not religious law.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Initiative and referendum support direct citizen participation in lawmaking.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Inferred; producerism understands conflict as producers against parasites, not as overlapping identity oppressions.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the conventional gendered household ideal.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Producerists claim to speak for the people against the few and shun left-right framing.

alienated-labor.rationale: The Knights claim workers deserve the fruit of their labor, but no theory of alienation is in the sources.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Anachronistic for the Gilded Age strand; modern right populists sometimes hold it, but producerism is not defined by it.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Omaha says the power of government is the people's power, which locates authority in the people.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Anachronistic; sources have nothing on workplace harassment.

social-market-economy.rationale: Omaha rejects laissez-faire, but a social-market compromise of competition rules and protection is not discussed.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Inferred from the republican nation, though the platforms are silent; Omaha opposes private armies, not the national forces.

rich-first.rationale: The Knights oppose concentrated gain, so allowing some to grow rich first does not fit.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Anachronistic; blocs did not exist, and no foreign policy appears in the platforms.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Producerism arose as opposition to idle inherited privilege, so hereditary succession in office is incompatible with it.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Omaha and the sub-treasury plan aim to give farmers credit at low interest through government.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Anachronistic; producerists favor debtors against creditors but the IMF did not exist.

property-franchise.rationale: Omaha asks for a fair, free ballot for the plain people and attacks wealth's control of politics, so a property qualification contradicts it.

domination-women-nature.rationale: An ecofeminist idea absent from the sources.

reification.rationale: A Marxist-Lukacsian idea absent from producerism.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Omaha laments corruption of the franchise, but ownership of the press is not in the sources.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Inferred from Omaha's demand for fair, secure elections and its attack on corrupt officials; rule by announced law fits, but the sources do not discuss decrees.

racial-franchise.rationale: Southern Populists were divided between biracial voting and disenfranchisement, and the platform demands a free ballot without racial terms.

online-participation.rationale: Anachronistic, but the movement's later support for initiative and referendum favors direct participation while nothing speaks to the internet.

open-government-data.rationale: Anachronistic; a direct-democracy movement might like transparency, but nothing says so.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Anti-Catholicism existed in parts of the movement, but no law on marriage appears in the sources.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Some Populists blamed Jewish financiers, but the platforms do not propose boycotts.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Anachronistic; Populist democratic reform ran through direct election and later initiative and referendum.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Not discussed; Populists included both modernists and fundamentalists.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Knights preamble warns that the concentration of wealth threatens the pauperization and degradation of the toiling masses.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Anachronistic; no basis in the sources.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Populism had many evangelical members, and no platform suggests state promotion of atheism.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Producerists sought to reform the state, and the Knights opposed only convict contract labor, not law enforcement itself.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Not discussed; Populists sought majority rule through the ballot.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Gilded Age producerists wanted state action on money and railroads, but their view on relief for the poor is not recorded.

term-limits.rationale: Omaha limits the president and vice president to one term, which supports limits on office.

vote-delegation.rationale: Liquid delegation is a modern device; producerists backed direct voting but never discussed delegating votes to trusted proxies.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: A modern concern with no connection to the Gilded Age sources, so the stance is unknowable from them.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Populism included women activists, but its denominations differed on women clergy, and the platforms are silent.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The gendered household ideal points against it while women's active party and union roles point toward it, so adherents split.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Omaha opposes alien land ownership and wants stricter immigration, so extending the vote to foreign residents conflicts with it.

rent-control.rationale: Producerists valued small owners, who might be landlords or tenants, so adherents are split.

abolish-ip.rationale: Inferred from the producerist respect for the inventor and producer's reward, though patents were not a platform plank.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Nothing in the civic-republican Populist program suggests drilled youth movements; inferred.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Anachronistic; the platforms contain no defense policy and nothing to infer a stand on nuclear basing from.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement's home-oriented outlook might favor it, but no source says so.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Not in the Gilded Age sources; the Populist record on Native Americans and minorities is mixed, so no stance is inferable.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Omaha states that every dollar taken from industry without an equivalent is robbery, and the Knights tie reward to productive labor.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Inferred from the republican and Jacksonian tradition valuing self-defense; pacifism is not in the sources.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Omaha appeals to the founding republic, but no ancient-continuity doctrine is recorded.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Inferred from the producer image resting on fixed gendered roles; no source states it.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the producer ideal's fixed gendered household.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Producerist rhetoric honors labor and the republic's founders rather than martyrs for the nation; no source takes a side.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Populist rhetoric was often millenarian, framing politics as a moral crusade, but doctrines varied.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: A diaspora-nationalist question with no counterpart.

culture-before-state.rationale: Omaha puts political and economic reform first, which implies the state before cultural renewal.

god-not-male.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from conventional Protestant language in the era.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Anachronistic; Populist religion was conventional Protestant, so this is inferred at low confidence.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Omaha limits alien landholding but does not propose majority control of the economy.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: A minority-nationality question absent from the sources.

independent-unions.rationale: Omaha is hostile to employer and state forces against workers.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Producerists are not socialists in the strict sense, so the claim is not theirs.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Omaha demands public ownership of railroads, telegraph and telephone, which extends by analogy to local water and transport, but local utilities were not named.

second-chamber.rationale: Omaha demands direct election of senators rather than abolishing the upper house, so a second chamber is accepted but not defended.

municipal-property.rationale: Omaha proposes national ownership of railroads and telegraph and individual farms, not municipal ownership of the means of production.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Populists wanted a stronger national government, not weak confederations of towns.

family-wage.rationale: The Knights platform seeks weekly full-money wages and shorter hours so workers can live decently with leisure, in line with the producer supporting a household.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Anachronistic regulation question; producerists favored regulating corporations but never discussed medicine approval.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Anachronistic; producerism offers no doctrine on science funding, so adherents would be split.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Anachronistic; producerists want public control of money, which implies traceable state currency, but the question is modern.

online-anonymity.rationale: Anachronistic; nothing in the sources about identity or communication privacy.

person-over-state.rationale: Producerists claim government is the people's tool, and they do not discuss the individual as an end.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Populist rhetoric was often religious, but sources record no doctrine on human nature.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Omaha empowers the national government, but does not address regional autonomy.

gm-crops.rationale: Anachronistic; farmers welcomed productive methods but nothing says so.

dense-cities.rationale: Inferred from the agrarian celebration of rural producers against urban finance; no source states it.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Southern Populists were divided between biracial coalition and white supremacy.

racial-pride.rationale: Same divide: white-supremacist Populists would agree, biracial ones would not, so there is no common view.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: The platforms do not address war aims, and Populists split over the 1898 war.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Not applicable to a US movement.

communal-electorates.rationale: Omaha demands a free, equal ballot, which rejects separate electorates.

free-public-college.rationale: Anachronistic; producerists favored government help for farmers and workers, but nothing on tuition appears in the platforms.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Anachronistic; producerists favor graduated income tax for revenue and had no environmental tax doctrine.

future-generations.rationale: Omaha calls land the people's inheritance for future settlers, which supports a duty of stewardship, though not about the Earth's damage.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Women were active in Populism and the Knights, but no source claims they bring distinct values.

arms-reduction.rationale: The platforms do not discuss armaments, and Populists were mainly concerned with money, land and railroads.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Transparency demands in Omaha relate to elections, not treaties, so no stance is recorded.

capital-controls.rationale: Omaha restricts foreign land ownership and wants government-issued money, but does not call for controls on capital flows.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Omaha condemns private armed forces like the Pinkertons, which supports public control of force, but this is not framed as a disarmament rule.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Inferred from the national outlook of producerism; refusal to fight is not endorsed in the sources.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The Knights promoted organization and arbitration of disputes between workers and employers, which fits collective setting of terms.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Anachronistic; producerists want fair pay from the market and cheap credit, not top-ups.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Omaha wants government revenue limited to expenses and money supply expanded, which leaves no clear stance.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Omaha's reform program concerns the domestic economy.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Omaha seeks to retake and use the existing government through elections, not to destroy it.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Not addressed; the programs are specific rather than experimental.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Omaha treats land as the people's inheritance, not as capital to be priced.

sacred-nation.rationale: Patriotic republican rhetoric appears, but not a sacred-nation doctrine.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Anachronistic; producerists favored debtors versus creditors, which might imply support, but the issue did not exist.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Omaha-era farmers saw eastern finance and railroads as exploiting the West and South, which matches the claim, though not in those terms.

shared-human-nature.rationale: The Knights ground rights in common moral worth of producers, which implies a shared human nature, though it is not discussed in those terms.

public-service-media.rationale: Anachronistic; Omaha wants public ownership of telegraph and telephone, but not public broadcasting.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Producerism was a Gilded Age economic creed that took no stand on religious truth; adherents were split.

farm-price-support.rationale: Farmers were central producers and the People's Party backed government credit, public purchase and the sub-treasury plan against moneylenders.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Anachronistic; no basis in the sources for a position.

workers-own-party.rationale: Producerists left the old parties for independent labour and farmer parties: the Knights of Labor and the People's Party.

ban-fgm.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the Knights' equal-pay and reform commitments, with no known defence of the practice.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The Knights of Labor demanded equal pay for equal work for both sexes; inferred extension to property, though the producer ideal was also gendered.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Not addressed; no basis in the sources.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Producerists wanted public control of key networks and curbs on monopolies, not a private-lawsuit regime; inferred.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: The Omaha Platform pushes direct popular democracy against elites, so an official role for hereditary chiefs is unlikely; inferred.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Not addressed; adherents have no common position.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Not addressed; the producerist hostility to parasites is economic and says nothing on sentencing.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: The Omaha Platform sought to restrict immigration and later strands were nativist; inferred, not stated.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Knights of Labor favoured organisation of all producers, but the sources never address compulsory dues, so adherents are split.

voter-id.rationale: The Omaha Platform stresses honest elections but never discusses ID checks; inferred split.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The Knights of Labor admitted workers across creeds and were non-sectarian; inferred from that.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The Omaha Platform demands real popular rule through direct election of senators, initiative and referendum, beyond mere elections.

premarital-sex.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the moralised 'virtuous producer' ideal of the era.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the Omaha Platform's hostility to monopoly control of communication networks.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the platform's preference for concrete public provision such as government money and public ownership.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Knights of Labor demanded equal pay for equal work for both sexes, from which equal political rights are inferred; many Populists were split.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the era's producerist reliance on churches and a gendered producer ideal.

race-social-construct.rationale: Anachronistic; the sources note producerism was often racialized, but the statement was not an issue in the period.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred split between pro-equality Knights and the platform's silence on state agencies.

homestead-ownership.rationale: The Omaha Platform wants reclaimed railroad land held for actual settlers only, so land belongs to those who work it.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Inferred: the 19th-century strand never addressed international tribunals and adherents' hostility to elites and foreign entanglements cuts both ways.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Inferred: producerists were often Protestant but the sources take no stance on scripture, and adherents were split.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Inferred from the Knights of Labor demand for equal pay for equal work of both sexes; the statement itself is anachronistic.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Inferred: producerists wanted public ownership of key networks but distrusted bureaucracy and never backed a planned economy.

indirect-election.rationale: The Omaha Platform demands direct popular election of senators, against selection by legislatures.

national-church-status.rationale: Inferred from the republican, anti-privilege outlook; the sources do not mention established churches.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Inferred: the strand's producer identity was often nativist and focused on one national people, not on minority territorial rights.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Inferred from the strand's direct-democracy commitment to settling questions by popular vote.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Inferred: the sources never address decolonisation and nothing in producerist principles settles it.

simple-living.rationale: Inferred from the producer ideal of thrift, honest labour and the self-reliant farm, not from a stated programme.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Inferred from the settler-friendly land stance of the Omaha Platform, which put land for actual settlers first.

equal-conscription.rationale: Inferred: the sources do not discuss conscription and nothing in the principles decides it.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Gilded Age producerists framed land as the people's heritage but not as a spiritual national bond; split on nativist versus class framings.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Not addressed; producerism stresses republican rights of working people, so state killing without trial is inferred to be rejected.

close-ties-china.rationale: Not addressed; 19th-century producerists were hostile to Chinese labour and to foreign finance, so closeness to China is inferred to be rejected.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Not addressed; producerism concerned domestic producers, and the question does not map to its class framing.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: The Omaha Platform calls land, including all natural sources of wealth, the heritage of the people, to be held by actual settlers, though it does not demand compensation.

self-ownership.rationale: Producerism prizes the worker's right to the full fruit of their labour, which is close to self-ownership, but it also backs collective action and state power.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Not addressed directly; producerists favoured a graduated income tax and attacked burdens on working people, so cutting taxes on daily goods is inferred.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Not addressed; producerists favoured broad public services but resented support for the idle, so adherents are split.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: The People's Party was itself a party and the Knights an organisation, so bypassing parties and groups is inferred to be rejected, though populists attacked party machines.

no-business-privileges.rationale: The Omaha Platform attacks corporations, railroads and monopolies for privileges and demands that land held beyond need be reclaimed and key networks go public.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Not addressed; producerist class politics cut across denominations, so mild agreement is inferred.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Not addressed; producerists embraced technology in the telegraph and railroads under public control while idealising the yeoman past, so it is split.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Not addressed; the Knights backed equal pay for equal work, but nothing speaks to divorce law.

national-resource-control.rationale: The Omaha Platform demands that land held by aliens be reclaimed and that alien ownership be prohibited, and wants key networks publicly owned.

missingStatements.text: People who profit from money-lending, speculation or trading without producing anything are a drain on those who produce wealth.
missingStatements.rationale: The Omaha Platform calls every dollar taken from industry without an equivalent robbery, and producerism defines itself against idle bankers and land speculators.

missingStatements.text: Land should be held only by those who use it, not by speculators, corporations or foreigners.
missingStatements.rationale: Both the Omaha Platform and the Knights of Labor platform demand reclaiming excess corporate and alien holdings for actual settlers.

notes: Strands differ on race, immigration and the poor: proprietary producerism (farmers, artisans) and industrial producerism (wage workers) differ on co-operatives and profit, white Populists often backed Chinese exclusion while others urged biracial cooperation, and modern right-populist producerism adds hostility to welfare recipients. Sources do not document most cultural and foreign-policy statements, so those are low confidence.
